newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kohl upbeat on NATO expansion after Yeltsin talks.
newsitem.headline: Kohl upbeat on NATO expansion after Yeltsin talks.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Saturday after talks with President Boris Yeltsin he expected to settle differences of opinion with Russia over NATO expansion in the course of this year.

Kohl, who met Yeltsin at a state hunting lodge outside Moscow, was the first Western leader to visit the Russian president since his heart bypass surgery in November. He said Yeltsin seemed fit and alert.

"There are still some differences of opinion," he told a news conference, referring to Russia's strong objections to plans to grant membership of the western defence alliance to former communist states in eastern Europe.
"But we evaluated a couple of ideas which I will discuss with my NATO colleagues over the next couple of days on the telephone," he added, mentioning U.S. President Bill Clinton.
"I think that this year we will find a rational solution which will make NATO enlargement possible and will at the same time respect the security interests of all partners concerned."
Earlier, Yeltsin was quoted as saying that he and Kohl had agreed to continue discussions on NATO expansion.

"We sought a settlement of this issue. We agreed to continue discussion in the future on the theme 'Russia and NATO'," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky quoted the Russian leader as saying, according to Interfax and Itar-Tass news agencies.

Western leaders see Yeltsin's return to the Kremlin after a long absence caused by his illness and July's presidential election campaign as a chance to end to apparently shifting policy in Moscow on NATO enlargement.
Yeltsin, starting a series of international contacts after a long absence due to illness and the campaign for last July's presidential election, agreed to visit Germany in April.
The two leaders also agreed to cooperate closely ahead of the next meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) rich nations and Russia, scheduled for Denver, Colorado on June 20 to 22.
Both said they would work to reduce bureaucratic obstacles to trade and other economic ties between Russia and Germany.

Greeting Kohl at the Rus hunting lodge some 100 km (60 miles) west of Moscow, Yeltsin looked tired in television footage. But he seemed pleased to see the chancellor, whom he regards as a personal friend.

Kohl said Yeltsin seemed fit but that he had advised him to take things easy for now. The president seemed mentally very sharp, however, demonstrating a full grasp of the issues with a minimum of briefing materials.

Yastrzhembsky quoted Yeltsin as telling Kohl at the start of the talks: "I am glad, Helmut, that we are opening the New Year's international calendar with this meeting, with talks on issues of mutual interest to Germany and to Russia."
The discussions lasted about three hours including lunch.
The chancellor has been hoping his warm personal relations with Yeltsin and the close German ties with Russia -- Bonn is Moscow's biggest creditor -- can help settle the NATO issue.

Many western analysts say Russia has already reconciled itself to the first wave of NATO enlargement -- likely to include Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic -- but is taking a tough position in order to secure other concessions.

NATO foreign ministers agreed last month to issue invitations in July for the first former Soviet bloc countries to join the alliance, and at the same time establish relations giving Russia a role in shaping Europe's defence arrangements.

French President Jacques Chirac is also due in Moscow later this month and Clinton plans to meet Yeltsin in the United States in March. British Prime Minister John Major has also been invited to Russia but a date is yet to be set.
